questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: DNA Replication: The Semiconservative Outcome
questions.learningObjective: State what semiconservative replication means
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse asks which model Meselson and Stahl supported after one round in heavy nitrogen.

options.text: Each daughter duplex carries one old strand and one new strand.
Both daughter duplexes are entirely newly synthesised strands.
Old and new segments are scattered through each strand.
The original duplex stays intact and a new one forms beside it.
options.misconception: assumes the parental duplex is preserved whole

questions.explanation: Semiconservative replication keeps one parental strand in each daughter molecule. The conservative model would keep the original duplex intact, and the dispersive model would scatter segments.
questions.hint: One old strand joins one new strand.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: DNA Replication: Why a Primer Is Needed
questions.learningObjective: Explain why DNA polymerase needs a primer
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse compares enzyme rates: polymerase extends at 50 nucleotides per second but cannot start a chain.

options.text: It needs a template strand running in the opposite direction only.
options.misconception: confuses template direction with initiation requirement

options.text: It needs a free 3-prime hydroxyl group to add the next nucleotide.
It needs ATP hydrolysis to open the helix before each base.
options.misconception: confuses helicase energy use with polymerase initiation

options.text: It needs a completed strand to copy from before it can begin.
options.misconception: assumes synthesis must follow a finished strand

questions.explanation: DNA polymerase adds nucleotides only to a free 3-prime OH, so a short RNA primer must be laid down first. The template direction and helicase energy are separate concerns.
questions.hint: Polymerase extends; it does not initiate.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: DNA Replication: Antiparallel Strands and Direction of Synthesis
questions.learningObjective: Relate strand orientation to synthesis direction
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse reads a fork diagram and must label which nascent strand grows toward the fork.

options.text: Both strands grow toward the fork at equal rates.
The strand whose 5-prime end faces the fork grows toward it.
The strand whose 3-prime end faces the fork grows toward it.
Neither strand grows toward the fork; both grow away.
options.misconception: misreads fork movement as strand movement

questions.explanation: Polymerase synthesises 5-prime to 3-prime, so the leading strand with its 3-prime end toward the fork grows continuously toward the fork. The lagging strand grows away in fragments.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: DNA Replication: Okazaki Fragments
questions.learningObjective: Identify why Okazaki fragments form
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse spots a claim that Okazaki fragments are produced because the lagging template is read 3-prime to 5-prime.

options.text: The claim is wrong: fragments arise from proofreading failure.
options.misconception: attributes fragments to an unrelated process

options.text: The claim is right: reading 3-prime to 5-prime forces discontinuous synthesis.
options.misconception: accepts the flawed causal explanation as stated

options.text: The claim is partly right: only short fragments need primers.
options.misconception: confuses primer need with fragment cause

options.text: The claim is wrong: fragments arise because synthesis is 5-prime to 3-prime on an antiparallel template.

questions.explanation: The lagging template is indeed read 3-prime to 5-prime, but that is normal; fragments arise because polymerase can only add 5-prime to 3-prime, so it must reinitiate repeatedly. Proofreading is separate.
questions.hint: Template reading direction is not the cause.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: DNA Replication: Unwinding the Duplex
questions.learningObjective: Design an experiment to test helicase function
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse must plan a control to show that unwinding at a fork requires ATP.

answer.exemplar: Compare fork unwinding in a reaction with ATP versus an identical reaction with a non-hydrolysable ATP analogue, measuring strand separation by gel mobility shift.

questions.explanation: A non-hydrolysable analogue isolates the energy requirement: if unwinding stalls without ATP hydrolysis, helicase depends on ATP. Gel mobility shift reports strand separation directly.
questions.hint: Swap ATP for a non-hydrolysable analogue.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: DNA Replication: Proofreading at the Growing End
questions.learningObjective: Explain how proofreading lowers error rate
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse explains why a polymerase with 3-prime exonuclease activity makes fewer mistakes.

answer.exemplar: The 3-prime exonuclease removes a mismatched nucleotide just added, allowing reinsertion of the correct base before synthesis continues, so the final error rate drops by orders of magnitude.

questions.explanation: Proofreading excises the wrong base immediately after misincorporation. Re-synthesis then inserts the correct base, sharply reducing the net error rate.
questions.hint: Wrong base out, right base in.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: DNA Replication: The End Replication Problem
questions.learningObjective: Compute how many bases are lost per round
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse notes a primer of 10 bases is removed from a chromosome end each replication round. How many bases are lost after 3 rounds?
questions.explanation: Each round removes one 10-base primer, so 3 rounds remove 30 bases total. Telomerase can compensate in some cells.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: DNA Replication: Time Needed to Copy a Genome
questions.learningObjective: Estimate replication time from rate and size
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse estimates copy time for a 3 billion base genome at 50 bases per second on one fork.

options.text: About 2 days on a single fork at that rate.
options.misconception: underestimates genome size by three orders

options.text: About 2 years on a single fork at that rate.
About 2 hours on a single fork at that rate.
About 2 minutes on a single fork at that rate.
options.misconception: treats the rate as bases per millisecond

questions.explanation: 3e9 bases divided by 50 bases per second is 6e7 seconds, about 1.9 years. Real cells use thousands of forks in parallel.
questions.hint: Divide bases by rate, then convert seconds.

questions.topic: Coding Sequences: Length from Protein Length
questions.learningObjective: Convert protein length to coding DNA length
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse notes a protein of 300 amino acids. How many bases code for it, excluding stop?
questions.explanation: Each amino acid needs one codon of 3 bases, so 300 times 3 equals 900 bases. The stop codon adds 3 more if included.

questions.topic: Copying Fidelity: Error Rate Scaled to a Genome
questions.learningObjective: Scale an error rate to a whole genome
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse uses an error rate of 1 in 1e9 bases. How many errors in a 3e9 base genome?
questions.explanation: 3e9 bases times 1e-9 errors per base gives 3 expected errors. Proofreading reduces this further in vivo.
questions.hint: Multiply genome size by error rate.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Lagging Strand: Counting Primers
questions.learningObjective: Count primers on a lagging strand
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse counts Okazaki fragments of 1000 bases on a 5000 base lagging strand. How many RNA primers are needed?
questions.explanation: Each fragment needs one primer, and 5000 divided by 1000 is 5 fragments, so 5 primers. The leading strand needs one primer separately.
questions.hint: Divide strand length by fragment length.

questions.explanation: One half-life leaves half the molecules, so the fraction is 0.5. After 12 hours it would be 0.25.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Transcription: Inferring the Start Time
questions.learningObjective: Infer transcription start from signal timing
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse sees a reporter signal rise 2 minutes after a trigger. Transcription plus translation take 2 minutes total.

options.text: Translation finished before transcription began.
options.misconception: confuses the order of transcription and translation

options.text: Transcription must have started 2 minutes before the trigger.
options.misconception: reverses cause and effect in timing

options.text: Transcription likely started immediately after the trigger.
The signal rise is unrelated to the trigger.

questions.explanation: A 2 minute delay matching the combined process time means transcription began right after the trigger. The other options misorder or ignore the timing.
questions.hint: Delay equals process time, so start is immediate.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: DNA Replication: Sequencing the Events at a Fork
questions.learningObjective: Order events at a replication fork
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse orders fork events: helicase unwinds, primase primes, polymerase extends, ligase joins.

options.text: Join, unwind, prime, extend is the correct order.
Prime, unwind, extend, join is the correct order.
Unwind, extend, prime, join is the correct order.
Unwind, prime, extend, join is the correct order.

questions.explanation: The helix must open before priming, priming before extension, and extension before ligation of fragments. The other orders violate dependencies.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Gene Expression: From DNA to a Working Protein
questions.learningObjective: Sequence the central dogma steps
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse lists the usual information flow from a gene to a functional protein.

options.text: Protein is reverse transcribed to RNA, then to DNA.
DNA is transcribed to RNA, then translated to protein.
RNA is replicated to DNA, then translated to protein.
DNA is translated directly to protein without RNA.

questions.explanation: The usual flow is DNA to RNA by transcription, then RNA to protein by translation. Reverse flow and skipping RNA are exceptions or errors.
questions.hint: DNA, RNA, protein in that order.

questions.topic: Transcription: The Promoter
questions.learningObjective: Identify the promoter's role
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse asks what a promoter sequence does for a gene.

options.text: It splices introns out of the primary transcript.
It terminates transcription when the gene is fully copied.
It recruits RNA polymerase to start transcription at the right place.
It translates the mRNA into amino acids.

questions.explanation: A promoter is a DNA region where RNA polymerase binds to initiate transcription. Termination, splicing, and translation are handled by other elements.

questions.topic: Transcription: Template and Coding Strands
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish template from coding strand
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse compares the two DNA strands at a transcribed gene.

options.text: Neither strand is read; RNA is copied from protein.
The coding strand is read 3-prime to 5-prime to make RNA.
options.misconception: swaps template and coding strand roles

options.text: Both strands are read to make two RNA copies.
The template strand is read 3-prime to 5-prime to make RNA.

questions.explanation: RNA polymerase reads the template strand 3-prime to 5-prime and synthesises RNA 5-prime to 3-prime. The coding strand matches the RNA sequence except T for U.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: RNA Processing: Introns and Exons
questions.learningObjective: Define intron and exon
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse asks which parts of a pre-mRNA remain in the mature message.

options.text: Introns remain; exons are removed by splicing.
Exons remain; introns are removed by splicing.
Both remain; splicing only adds a cap.
Neither remains; the message is rebuilt from DNA.

questions.explanation: Splicing removes introns and joins exons to produce mature mRNA. Capping and polyadenylation are separate modifications.
questions.hint: Exons are expressed; introns are intervening.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how one gene yields multiple proteins
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse asks how a single gene can produce several distinct proteins.

options.text: Each cell translates the same mRNA differently.
The DNA sequence is rewritten in each cell type.
Different exon combinations are spliced together in different cells.
The gene is duplicated for each protein variant.

questions.explanation: Alternative splicing selects different exon sets from one pre-mRNA, yielding multiple protein isoforms from one gene. DNA sequence and translation machinery stay the same.

questions.topic: Transcription: Why No Primer Is Needed
questions.learningObjective: Contrast transcription with replication initiation
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse asks why transcription does not need a primer.

options.text: Transcription copies from an RNA template that already has a 3-prime OH.
Transcription uses a DNA primer made by primase.
The promoter itself acts as the primer.
RNA polymerase can initiate synthesis de novo on a template.

questions.explanation: RNA polymerase initiates RNA synthesis without a primer, unlike DNA polymerase. Primase and promoters serve different roles.
questions.hint: RNA polymerase starts on its own.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Translation: Charging the Transfer RNA
questions.learningObjective: Describe aminoacyl-tRNA charging
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse asks what charges a tRNA with its amino acid.

options.text: The ribosome attaches the amino acid during elongation.
options.misconception: confuses charging with ribosomal peptide bond formation

options.text: An aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase links amino acid to tRNA using ATP.
RNA polymerase charges tRNA during transcription.
A DNA ligase joins amino acid to tRNA.
options.misconception: imports a replication enzyme into translation

questions.explanation: Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases attach the correct amino acid to each tRNA in an ATP-dependent reaction. The ribosome uses but does not charge tRNAs.
questions.hint: Synthetase plus ATP, not the ribosome.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Translation: Codon and Anticodon Pairing
questions.learningObjective: Pair a codon with its anticodon
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse matches codon AUG to its tRNA anticodon.

options.text: The anticodon is TAC, using DNA bases.
options.misconception: uses DNA thymine instead of RNA uracil

options.text: The anticodon is AUG, identical to the codon.
The anticodon is UAC, complementary and antiparallel to AUG.
The anticodon is CAU, reversed but not complementary.

questions.explanation: Codon and anticodon are complementary and antiparallel, with U replacing T in RNA, so AUG pairs with UAC. Identity, DNA bases, or mere reversal are wrong.
questions.hint: Complement and antiparallel, U for T.

options.text: The S site holds the peptide-bearing tRNA.
The A site holds the peptide-bearing tRNA.
options.misconception: confuses A site with P site

options.text: The E site holds the peptide-bearing tRNA.
options.misconception: confuses E site with P site

options.text: The P site holds the peptide-bearing tRNA.

questions.explanation: The P site carries the tRNA attached to the growing peptide, the A site receives the next aminoacyl-tRNA, and the E site releases empty tRNA. There is no S site.

Label first appears in DNA, then in RNA.

options.text: Label appears only in protein, never in RNA.
Label first appears in RNA, then moves to protein.

questions.learningObjective: Explain nonsense-mediated decay

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: DNA Replication: Why a Primer Is Needed
questions.learningObjective: Predict consequence of primase failure
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse spots a claim that without primase, replication stops because polymerase cannot unwind DNA.

options.text: The claim is right: primase unwinds DNA for polymerase.
The claim is wrong: without primase, polymerase lacks a 3-prime OH to extend.
The claim is partly right: only the leading strand needs primase.
The claim is wrong: primase proofreads mismatches.

questions.explanation: Primase synthesises RNA primers; without them polymerase has no 3-prime OH to extend. Unwinding is helicase's job, not primase's.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: DNA Replication: Antiparallel Strands and Direction of Synthesis
questions.learningObjective: Identify the leading strand
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse reads a fork moving right and must pick the leading strand.

options.text: The bottom strand always leads regardless of orientation.
The top strand with its 5-prime end pointing right is leading.
The top strand with its 3-prime end pointing right is leading.
Both strands lead in opposite directions.
options.misconception: confuses bidirectional fork with strand leading

questions.explanation: The leading strand is the one whose template runs 3-prime to 5-prime toward the fork, allowing continuous 5-prime to 3-prime synthesis. Orientation determines leading, not top or bottom.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: DNA Replication: Okazaki Fragments
questions.learningObjective: State the function of DNA ligase on fragments
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse asks what joins Okazaki fragments into one strand.

options.text: Primase joins fragments by adding RNA.
DNA polymerase joins fragments by extending primers.
Helicase joins fragments while unwinding.
DNA ligase seals nicks between adjacent fragments.

questions.explanation: DNA ligase forms phosphodiester bonds at nicks between Okazaki fragments. Polymerase, helicase, and primase perform other tasks.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: DNA Replication: Unwinding the Duplex
questions.learningObjective: Identify the role of single-strand binding protein
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse asks what keeps separated strands apart at a fork.

options.text: DNA ligase keeps them apart by sealing nicks.
Single-strand binding proteins coat and stabilise them.
Primase keeps them apart by adding primers.
Helicase keeps them apart by reannealing strands.
options.misconception: confuses helicase unwinding with strand stabilisation

questions.explanation: Single-strand binding proteins coat exposed strands to prevent reannealing and protect them. Ligase, primase, and helicase do not serve this role.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: DNA Replication: Proofreading at the Growing End
questions.learningObjective: Predict effect of losing proofreading
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse spots a claim that loss of 3-prime exonuclease raises the mutation rate a thousand-fold.

options.text: The claim is wrong: only 5-prime exonuclease affects fidelity.
The claim is wrong: proofreading loss has no effect on mutation rate.
The claim is plausible: proofreading loss greatly increases errors.
The claim is wrong: mismatch repair replaces proofreading entirely.

questions.explanation: Loss of 3-prime exonuclease proofreading markedly raises mutation rate, though mismatch repair still operates. It is not negligible or replaced.
questions.hint: Proofreading is a major fidelity layer.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: DNA Replication: The End Replication Problem
questions.learningObjective: Explain telomerase action
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse asks which enzyme extends chromosome ends.

options.text: Ligase extends ends by sealing nicks.
DNA polymerase adds repeats using a DNA template.
Helicase extends ends by unwinding.
Telomerase adds telomeric repeats using its RNA template.

questions.explanation: Telomerase is a reverse transcriptase that extends telomeres using its own RNA template. Polymerase, helicase, and ligase do not perform this.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: DNA Replication: Time Needed to Copy a Genome
questions.learningObjective: Compute number of forks needed
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse needs to copy 3e9 bases in 8 hours using forks at 50 bases per second. How many forks are needed?
questions.explanation: Required rate is 3e9 divided by 28800 seconds, about 104167 bases per second; divided by 50 gives about 20833 forks. Rounding gives 20834.
questions.hint: Divide total bases by seconds, then by fork rate.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Coding Sequences: Length from Protein Length
questions.learningObjective: Include stop codon in coding length
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse notes a protein of 100 amino acids including stop. How many bases in its coding sequence?
questions.explanation: 100 codons times 3 bases equals 300, plus 3 for the stop codon gives 303. The stop is an extra codon.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Copying Fidelity: Error Rate Scaled to a Genome
questions.learningObjective: Compare error rates with and without proofreading
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse compares 1e-5 without proofreading versus 1e-9 with. Errors in 3e9 bases without proofreading?
questions.explanation: 3e9 times 1e-5 equals 30000 errors without proofreading, versus 3 with. Proofreading reduces errors by four orders of magnitude.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Lagging Strand: Counting Primers
questions.learningObjective: Count primers including the leading strand
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse counts 5 lagging fragments of 1000 bases plus one leading strand. Total primers?
questions.explanation: Five lagging fragments need 5 primers, and the leading strand needs 1, totalling 6. Each strand initiation needs a primer.
questions.hint: Add one primer for the leading strand.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Messenger RNA Decay: Reading a Half-Life
questions.learningObjective: Compute remaining after two half-lives
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse tracks mRNA half-life 4 hours. Fraction remaining after 8 hours?
questions.explanation: Two half-lives reduce the amount by half twice, leaving 0.25. Exponential decay halves each period.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Transcription: Inferring the Start Time
questions.learningObjective: Infer start time from a delayed signal
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse sees a reporter rise 5 minutes after trigger, with transcription taking 3 and translation 2 minutes.

options.text: Transcription started 3 minutes before the trigger.
Transcription started right after the trigger.
Translation finished before transcription began.
The trigger is unrelated to expression.

questions.explanation: A 5 minute delay equals 3 plus 2 minutes, so transcription began immediately after the trigger. The other options misorder or ignore the timing.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: DNA Replication: Sequencing the Events at a Fork
questions.learningObjective: Identify a missing step in a proposed sequence
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse spots a proposed fork sequence that omits primase and goes straight from unwinding to extension.

options.text: The sequence is valid because helicase provides the primer.
The sequence is valid because polymerase can start de novo.
options.misconception: confuses DNA polymerase with RNA polymerase

options.text: The sequence is invalid because polymerase needs a primer before extension.
The sequence is invalid because ligase must act first.

questions.explanation: DNA polymerase cannot initiate without a primer, so primase must act after unwinding and before extension. Polymerase is not de novo and helicase does not prime.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Gene Expression: From DNA to a Working Protein
questions.learningObjective: Explain the role of chaperones
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse asks what helps a newly made protein reach its functional shape.

options.text: Chaperones degrade the mRNA after translation.
Chaperones splice introns from the mRNA.
Chaperones replicate the DNA template.
Chaperones assist folding and prevent aggregation.

questions.explanation: Chaperones guide proper protein folding and prevent misfolding or aggregation. Splicing, replication, and decay are unrelated to folding.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Transcription: The Promoter
questions.learningObjective: Predict effect of promoter mutation
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse spots a claim that a promoter mutation always increases transcription.

options.text: The claim is right: all promoter mutations boost output.
The claim is wrong: promoter mutations can increase or decrease transcription.
The claim is right: promoter mutations only affect translation.
The claim is wrong: promoter mutations delete the gene.

questions.explanation: Promoter mutations can strengthen or weaken RNA polymerase binding, raising or lowering transcription. They do not uniformly boost output or delete genes.
questions.hint: Promoter strength can go either way.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Transcription: Template and Coding Strands
questions.learningObjective: Find the mRNA sequence from the coding strand
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse has coding strand 5-prime ATG 3-prime and must give the mRNA.

options.text: UAC, complementary to the coding strand.
options.misconception: complements instead of matching coding strand

options.text: ATG, identical to the coding strand.
AUG, with U replacing T.
TAC, using DNA bases.

questions.explanation: The coding strand sequence matches mRNA except T becomes U, so ATG becomes AUG. Complementing or keeping T is incorrect.
questions.hint: Coding strand matches mRNA, U for T.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: RNA Processing: Introns and Exons
questions.learningObjective: Predict effect of a splice-site mutation
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse spots a claim that a splice-site mutation only affects introns and never the protein.

options.text: The claim is wrong: splice mutations delete the whole gene.
The claim is right: splice sites only touch introns.
The claim is right: splicing never changes the protein.
The claim is wrong: mis-splicing can alter exons and the protein.

questions.explanation: Splice-site mutations can cause exon skipping or intron retention, changing the mRNA and protein. They do not always delete the gene.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: RNA Processing: Alternative Splicing
questions.learningObjective: Explain tissue-specific isoforms
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse asks why the same gene makes different protein isoforms in brain and liver.

options.text: The DNA sequence differs between tissues.
Different tissues use different splice patterns.
The genetic code differs between tissues.
Translation speed differs only.

questions.explanation: Alternative splicing patterns vary by tissue, producing distinct isoforms from one gene. DNA sequence and genetic code are the same in all cells.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Transcription: Why No Primer Is Needed
questions.learningObjective: Contrast primase and RNA polymerase initiation
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse explains why RNA polymerase can start without primase.

answer.exemplar: RNA polymerase initiates RNA chains de novo at a promoter, whereas DNA polymerase requires a free 3-prime OH provided by an RNA primer synthesised by primase.

questions.explanation: RNA polymerase does not need a primer to initiate, unlike DNA polymerase. This distinction separates transcription from replication initiation.
